newsitem.title: FRANCE: Seguin is right's last hope for French premier.
newsitem.headline: Seguin is right's last hope for French premier.

text.p: Socially minded Gaullist Philippe Seguin has emerged as the man to succeed outgoing Prime Minister Alain Juppe if the right manages to scrape through in Sunday's parliamentary election runoff.

Seguin and militant free-marketeer Alain Madelin have been thrust into the limelight as the improbable "dream team" to salvage the centre-right's chances after a left-wing upset in the election's first round of voting last Sunday.
Opinion polls have long shown Seguin, a recent convert to a single European Union currency, as favourite for prime minister if the centre-right wins. Madelin would be his finance minister.
The sudden focus on Seguin and Madelin followed Juppe's announcement on Monday in a bid to improve the centre-right's chances that he was bowing out whoever wins on Sunday.
Seguin's supporters say he is best placed to heed voters' warning that they want the fight for jobs to take precedence over austerity geared towards the planned EU single currency.
"Europe must become more democratic and make jobs, and in general people's happiness, its central concern. Today it could not care less and could ruin everything," Seguin said this week.
Seguin, the outgoing National Assembly speaker, is the only senior centre-right politician who has not been tarnished by holding office over the last four years.
But political analysts said the bizarre last-minute tandem could just as easily alienate voters by further blurring Chirac's unclear message about what policies he wants his government to follow.

Seguin, 54, a former social affairs minister, has toned down his rhetoric against the Maastricht treaty on greater EU economic and monetary union and and shifted closer to President Jacques Chirac's drive for the single European currency as he sensed a possible breakthrough.
France voted narrowly to sign the Maastricht treaty in a 1992 referendum when Seguin led the "no" camp. "This signature must be honoured. This problem is thus behind us," Seguin said.

His social Gaullism, with its emphasis on the role of the state in protecting the weak and jobless, has been a useful counterfoil at the hustings to the Juppe government's record of austerity, tax increases and record unemployment.
Seguin has also sought to distance himself from state economic "dirigisme" saying he supports "a tempered liberalism".
But EU partners and financial markets may wonder how far the anti-Maastricht leopard has really changed his spots.
And political sources say Chirac may have serious misgivings about promoting a man of such political unpredictability, robust temper and presidential ambition.
Seguin defied the leadership of his Gaullist RPR party and came within a whisker of turning voters against EU economic and monetary union in the Maastricht referendum.
An outstanding orator, he represented the anti-Maastricht camp in a crucial live television debate with Socialist president Francois Mitterrand who was ill with cancer.
Hoping to silence him with a largely ceremonial job, the RPR had Seguin elected National Assembly president in 1993 after emerging as the biggest party in a parliamentary election.
Instead, the rebel became an authoritarian and active speaker, trying to build up the Assembly's role, punishing absenteeism and reforming the parliamentary calendar.
His huge bearlike figure and deep voice became familiar to viewers as he scolded deputies like schoolchildren for rumpus in the twice-weekly televised assembly question time.

He used his high-profile position to become the social conscience of the centre-right coalition, accusing Balladur of capitulating to unemployment and comparing his policies to the Western powers' appeasement of Adolf Hitler in the run-up to World War Two.

When Chirac was elected president and appointed Juppe as prime minister, Seguin continued to warn that indiscriminate budget cuts would not pull France out of recession and advocated a more expansionary economic policy.

The popular satirical television show "Les Guignols" depicted Seguin in the speaker's chair behind and above Juppe, taunting the infuriated premier by repeating "It won't work" as he outlined his platform to the assembly.

Born in Tunis in 1943, Seguin never knew his father, who was killed in World War Two when he was a baby. Like many politicians, he attended the Ecole Nationale d'Administration and joined the office of centrist premier Raymond Barre in 1977.
